```bash
tc qdisc add dev eth0.50 root tbf \
  rate 5mbit \
  burst 10kb \
  latency 50ms
```

### Ethernet Switch Topology

**Star Topology (Recommended)**
```
Central TSN Switch (NXP SJA1110)
  Port 0: 1000BASE-T1 to Central Compute
  Port 1: 100BASE-T1 to FL Zone
  Port 2: 100BASE-T1 to FC Zone
  Port 3: 100BASE-T1 to FR Zone
  Port 4: 100BASE-T1 to C Zone
  Port 5: 100BASE-T1 to RL Zone
  Port 6: 100BASE-T1 to RC Zone
  Port 7: 100BASE-T1 to RR Zone
  Port 8: 100BASE-T1 to Diagnostics (OBD-II)
  Port 9: 100BASE-T1 to Telematics (V2X)
```

**Switch Configuration YAML**

```yaml
switch:
  model: NXP_SJA1110
  ports: 10
  mac_address: "00:04:9F:12:34:56"

  global_config:
    ptp_enabled: true
    ptp_domain: 0
    ptp_profile: automotive
    store_and_forward: true  # For TSN compliance

  port_config:
    - port_id: 0
      name: central_compute
      speed: 1000BASE-T1
      duplex: full
      vlan_mode: trunk
      allowed_vlans: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
      native_vlan: 10
      tsn_enabled: true
      tas_enabled: true
      ptp_role: master

    - port_id: 1
      name: fl_zone
      speed: 100BASE-T1
      duplex: full
      vlan_mode: access
      access_vlan: 60  # Body control
      tsn_enabled: false
      ptp_role: slave

    - port_id: 2
      name: fc_zone
      speed: 100BASE-T1
      duplex: full
      vlan_mode: trunk
      allowed_vlans: [10, 20]  # Safety + ADAS
      native_vlan: 20
      tsn_enabled: true
      tas_enabled: true
      ptp_role: slave

  vlan_database:
    - vlan_id: 10
      name: safety_critical
      priority: 7
      fdb_aging_time: 300

    - vlan_id: 20
      name: adas
      priority: 6
      fdb_aging_time: 300

    - vlan_id: 30
      name: infotainment
      priority: 5
      fdb_aging_time: 60

    - vlan_id: 50
      name: diagnostics
      priority: 1
      fdb_aging_time: 30

  qos_config:
    scheduler: strict_priority  # Higher priority always first
    traffic_classes: 8
    queue_mapping:
      - priority: 7
        queue: 7
        weight: 100
      - priority: 6
        queue: 6
        weight: 90
      - priority: 5
        queue: 5
        weight: 80
      # ... etc
```

### Bandwidth Calculation

**100BASE-T1 Link Budget**
```
Total bandwidth: 100 Mbps
Ethernet overhead: 20% (preamble, IPG, headers)
Usable bandwidth: 80 Mbps

Allocation example:
- Safety-critical (VLAN 10): 10 Mbps (12.5%)
- ADAS (VLAN 20): 40 Mbps (50%)
- Infotainment (VLAN 30): 20 Mbps (25%)
- Diagnostics (VLAN 50): 10 Mbps (12.5%)
```

**Camera Bandwidth Example**
```
Resolution: 1920 × 1080
Color depth: 24 bpp (RGB)
Frame rate: 30 fps
Compression: None (raw)

Raw bandwidth: 1920 × 1080 × 24 × 30 = 1.49 Gbps (needs 1000BASE-T1)

With H.264 compression (20:1):
Compressed bandwidth: 1.49 Gbps / 20 = 74.5 Mbps (fits in 100BASE-T1)
```

### Security (MACsec)

MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) provides hop-by-hop encryption on Ethernet links.

```yaml
macsec_config:
  interface: eth0
  encryption_mode: GCM-AES-256
  integrity_only: false  # Encrypt + authenticate
  key_exchange: MKA  # MACsec Key Agreement

  secure_channel:
    sci: "00:04:9F:12:34:56:00:01"  # Secure Channel Identifier
    transmit_sa: 0

```

### Testing and Validation

**Latency Test (ping with PTP timestamp)**

```bash
ping -c 100 -i 0.01 192.168.10.10  # 100 pings at 10ms interval
```

```bash
# Client (on zone controller)

```

**TSN Validation (tc-taprio test)**
```bash

tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent ffff: \
  flower ip_proto icmp \
  action skbedit priority 7

# Capture packets with tcpdump and verify transmission times
tcpdump -i eth0 -j adapter_unsynced -tt -n icmp
```

skills.name: automotive-security-network-security-zonal
skills.title: Network Security
skills.description: Expert in automotive Ethernet network security for zonal architectures including MACsec (802.1AE), IPsec, firewall rules, intrusion detection systems (IDS), secure gateways, and ISO 21434 compliance.
skills.content:
## 适用场景
- MACsec hop-by-hop encryption configuration
- IPsec end-to-end VPN tunnels for cloud connectivity
- Zone controller firewall rules and ACLs
- Intrusion Detection System (IDS) deployment
- Secure gateway implementation for zone isolation
- ISO 21434 threat analysis and risk assessment

## 相关标准
- ISO 21434 (Cybersecurity Engineering)
- IEEE 802.1AE (MACsec)
- IETF RFC 4301 (IPsec)
- IETF RFC 5996 (IKEv2)
- AUTOSAR Adaptive SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication)
- EVITA (E-safety Vehicle Intrusion Protected Applications)

## 约束
- MACsec mandatory for all inter-zone Ethernet links
- IPsec mandatory for cloud connectivity
- Firewall default policy: DENY (whitelist approach)
- IDS alert latency < 100ms
- Security log storage: 30 days retention
- ISO 21434 CAL (Cybersecurity Assurance Level) 3 or higher

## 推荐工具
- MACsec-capable hardware (NXP S32G, Marvell PHYs)
- IPsec stack (strongSwan, Libreswan)
- Firewall (iptables, nftables)
- IDS (Suricata, Snort, Zeek)
- SIEM (Splunk, ELK stack, Wazuh)
- Penetration testing (Metasploit, Kali Linux)

## 方法
## Network Security for Zonal Architectures

You are an expert in securing automotive Ethernet networks in zonal architectures, implementing defense-in-depth with MACsec, IPsec, firewalls, and intrusion detection.

### Security Threat Model for Zonal Architecture

**Attack Vectors**
1. **External attacks** (OBD-II, telematics, V2X)
2. **Supply chain attacks** (compromised sensors/actuators)
3. **Physical access** (USB, diagnostics port)
4. **Wireless attacks** (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular)
5. **Software vulnerabilities** (buffer overflow, injection)

**Assets to Protect**
- Safety-critical functions (brake, steering)
- Personal data (location, driver behavior)
- Intellectual property (vehicle firmware)
- Cloud credentials (OTA update keys)

**Security Goals**
- **Confidentiality**: Encrypt sensitive data
- **Integrity**: Detect message tampering
- **Authenticity**: Verify sender identity
- **Availability**: Prevent DoS attacks
- **Non-repudiation**: Audit trail of actions

### Defense-in-Depth Strategy

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 1: Physical Security                     │
│ - Tamper-resistant ECU enclosures              │
│ - Secure boot (prevent firmware modification)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 2: Network Segmentation                  │
│ - VLANs per security domain                    │
│ - Zone controllers as security gateways        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 3: Encryption (MACsec / IPsec)           │
│ - Hop-by-hop: MACsec between zones             │
│ - End-to-end: IPsec to cloud backend           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 4: Firewalls & Access Control            │
│ - Whitelist allowed traffic per zone           │
│ - Rate limiting (prevent DoS)                  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 5: Intrusion Detection (IDS)             │
│ - Anomaly detection (ML-based)                 │
│ - Signature-based detection (known attacks)    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 6: Security Monitoring & Logging         │
│ - SIEM (Security Information Event Management) │
│ - Forensic analysis of security events         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) - Hop-by-Hop Encryption

MACsec provides Layer 2 encryption and authentication between directly connected nodes (e.g., zone controller ↔ central switch).

**MACsec Configuration Example**

```yaml
# MACsec configuration for FC Zone Controller
macsec:
  interface: eth0
  mode: GCM-AES-256  # AES-256 in GCM mode
  encryption: true   # Encrypt + authenticate (vs integrity-only)
  replay_protect: true
  replay_window: 32  # Accept packets within 32 sequence numbers

  # Secure Channel (SC)
  secure_channel:
    sci: "00:04:9F:12:34:56:00:01"  # MAC + Port ID
    transmit_sa: 0  # Transmit Secure Association
    receive_sa: 0   # Receive Secure Association

  # Secure Association (SA) keys
  secure_associations:
    - sa_id: 0
      key: "0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF"
      active: true
      pn: 1  # Packet Number (for anti-replay)
      expiry_seconds: 86400  # Rotate key daily

    - sa_id: 1
      key: "FEDCBA9876543210FEDCBA9876543210FEDCBA9876543210FEDCBA9876543210"
      active: false  # Standby key for rotation
      pn: 1

  # Key Agreement Protocol (MKA - MACsec Key Agreement)
  mka:
    enabled: true
    hello_interval_ms: 2000
    lifetime_seconds: 6
    psk: "shared_secret_key_for_mka"  # Pre-shared key (or use 802.1X)
```

**Linux MACsec Setup**

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Configure MACsec on Linux (ip link command)

INTERFACE="eth0"
SCI="00049f1234560001"
KEY="0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF"

# Create MACsec interface
ip link add link $INTERFACE macsec0 type macsec \
    sci $SCI \
    encrypt on \
    send_sci on \
    replay on window 32

# Add transmit secure association (TX SA)
ip macsec add macsec0 tx sa 0 pn 1 on key 00 $KEY

# Add receive secure association (RX SA) for peer
PEER_SCI="00049f7654320001"
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address 00:04:9f:76:54:32
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address 00:04:9f:76:54:32 sa 0 pn 1 on key 00 $KEY

# Bring up interface
ip link set macsec0 up

# Assign IP address
ip addr add 192.168.10.10/24 dev macsec0
```

**MACsec Performance Impact**
- Latency overhead: +100-500 µs (hardware offload) or +1-5 ms (software)
- Bandwidth overhead: 32 bytes per frame (SecTAG + ICV)
- CPU usage: < 5% with hardware offload (NXP S32G, Marvell 88Q21xx)

### IPsec - End-to-End VPN

IPsec provides end-to-end encryption for traffic to cloud backend (OTA updates, telemetry).

**IPsec Tunnel Mode Configuration**

```yaml
# IPsec configuration for Central Compute → Cloud Backend
ipsec:
  mode: tunnel  # Tunnel mode (entire IP packet encrypted)
  protocol: ESP  # Encapsulating Security Payload (vs AH authentication-only)
  encryption: AES-256-GCM
  integrity: SHA-256-HMAC
  pfs: DH-group-14  # Perfect Forward Secrecy (Diffie-Hellman)

  # IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange) for key management
  ikev2:
    local_id: vehicle.oem.com
    remote_id: cloud.oem.com
    auth_method: PSK  # Pre-shared key (or use certificates)
    psk: "supersecret_vehicle_cloud_psk"
    dh_group: modp2048
    rekey_time_hours: 24

  # Security Association (SA)
  sa:
    local_subnet: 192.168.0.0/16  # Vehicle internal network
    remote_subnet: 10.0.0.0/8     # Cloud backend network
    local_gateway: 192.168.1.1    # Central compute Ethernet IP
    remote_gateway: 203.0.113.10  # Cloud VPN gateway public IP
    spi: 0x12345678  # Security Parameter Index
    lifetime_seconds: 3600
```

**strongSwan IPsec Configuration (Linux)**

```conf
# /etc/ipsec.conf
config setup
    charondebug="ike 2, knl 2, cfg 2"
    uniqueids=never

conn vehicle-to-cloud
    type=tunnel
    left=192.168.1.1         # Central compute IP
    leftsubnet=192.168.0.0/16
    leftid=@vehicle.oem.com
    right=203.0.113.10       # Cloud VPN gateway
    rightsubnet=10.0.0.0/8
    rightid=@cloud.oem.com
    authby=secret            # PSK authentication
    ike=aes256-sha256-modp2048!
    esp=aes256gcm16-sha256-modp2048!
    keyexchange=ikev2
    ikelifetime=24h
    lifetime=1h
    dpdaction=restart
    dpddelay=30s
    dpdtimeout=120s
    auto=start
```

```conf
# /etc/ipsec.secrets
@vehicle.oem.com @cloud.oem.com : PSK "supersecret_vehicle_cloud_psk"
```

### Firewall Rules (iptables / nftables)

**Zone Controller Firewall (Linux nftables)**

```nft
# /etc/nftables.conf - FC Zone Controller Firewall
table inet filter {
    # Input chain: Traffic destined to this zone controller
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

        # Allow established/related connections
        ct state established,related accept

        # Allow loopback
        iif lo accept

        # Allow SOME/IP from central compute (192.168.10.1)
        ip saddr 192.168.10.1 udp dport 30501 accept
        ip saddr 192.168.10.1 tcp dport 30501 accept

        # Allow diagnostics (UDS) from OBD-II gateway (192.168.50.1)
        ip saddr 192.168.50.1 tcp dport 13400 accept

        # Allow ICMP ping (for network testing)
        icmp type echo-request limit rate 10/second accept

        # Log dropped packets
        log prefix "INPUT-DROP: " drop
    }

    # Forward chain: Traffic routed through zone controller (gateway function)
    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;

        # Allow CAN → Ethernet forwarding (safety-critical only)
        iifname "can0" oifname "eth0" ip daddr 192.168.10.0/24 accept

        # Block Ethernet → CAN (prevent attacks on local bus)
        iifname "eth0" oifname "can0" drop

        # Rate limit forwarded traffic (prevent DoS)
        limit rate 100 mbytes/second accept

        log prefix "FORWARD-DROP: " drop
    }

    # Output chain: Traffic originating from zone controller
    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;

        # Allow all outbound (zone controller is trusted)
    }
}

# NAT table (if zone controller acts as gateway)
table inet nat {
    chain postrouting {
        type nat hook postrouting priority 100; policy accept;

        # Masquerade local CAN network when forwarding to Ethernet
        oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.100.0/24 masquerade
    }
}
```

**Rate Limiting (Token Bucket)**

```yaml
# Rate limiter to prevent DoS attacks
rate_limiters:
  - name: diagnostics_rate_limit
    target: diagnostics VLAN (50)
    algorithm: token_bucket
    cir_mbps: 5   # Committed Information Rate
    cbs_kb: 10    # Committed Burst Size
    action_exceed: drop

  - name: some_ip_flood_protection
    target: SOME/IP service discovery (UDP 30490)
    algorithm: token_bucket
    cir_pps: 100  # 100 packets/second max
    action_exceed: drop_and_log
```

### Intrusion Detection System (IDS)

**IDS Architecture for Zonal Vehicle**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Central Compute (IDS Aggregator)            │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ IDS Engine (Suricata / Snort)           │ │
│ │ - Signature-based detection             │ │
│ │ - Anomaly detection (ML model)          │ │
│ │ - Correlation engine                    │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└───────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
            │ (Aggregates IDS alerts from zones)
    ┌───────┴───────┬───────────┬───────────┐
    │               │           │           │
┌───▼───┐      ┌───▼───┐  ┌───▼───┐  ┌───▼───┐
│ FL    │      │ FC    │  │  C    │  │ RL    │
│ Zone  │      │ Zone  │  │ Zone  │  │ Zone  │
│ IDS   │      │ IDS   │  │ IDS   │  │ IDS   │
└───────┘      └───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
(Lightweight IDS sensors in each zone)
```

**Signature-Based Detection (Suricata Rules)**

```yaml
# suricata.rules - Example rules for automotive IDS
# Detect SOME/IP service discovery flood
alert udp any any -> any 30490 (msg:"SOME/IP SD Flood Detected"; \
    threshold: type both, track by_src, count 100, seconds 1; \
    sid:1000001; rev:1;)

# Detect unauthorized UDS diagnostic request
alert tcp !192.168.50.0/24 any -> any 13400 (msg:"Unauthorized UDS Request"; \
    content:"|10 01|"; offset:0; depth:2; \
    sid:1000002; rev:1;)

# Detect CAN message injection (invalid source MAC)
alert eth any any -> any any (msg:"Spoofed CAN Gateway MAC"; \
    content:"|00 04 9F|"; offset:0; depth:3; \
    sid:1000003; rev:1;)

# Detect replay attack (duplicate packet number in MACsec)
alert eth any any -> any any (msg:"MACsec Replay Attack"; \
    content:"|08 E8|"; offset:12; depth:2; \  # MACsec EtherType
    threshold: type both, track by_src, count 5, seconds 1; \
    sid:1000004; rev:1;)
```

**Anomaly Detection (ML-based)**

```python
# anomaly_detector.py - ML-based IDS for automotive Ethernet
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from scapy.all import sniff, Ether, IP, UDP

# Train model on normal traffic (baseline)
def train_model(pcap_file):
    packets = rdpcap(pcap_file)
    features = extract_features(packets)

    model = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=42)
    model.fit(features)
    return model

# Extract features from packet (for ML)
def extract_features(packets):
    features = []
    for pkt in packets:
        if IP in pkt and UDP in pkt:
            feature_vector = [
                len(pkt),                      # Packet size
                pkt[IP].src,                   # Source IP (as int)
                pkt[IP].dst,                   # Dest IP (as int)
                pkt[UDP].sport,                # Source port
                pkt[UDP].dport,                # Dest port
                pkt.time,                      # Timestamp
            ]
            features.append(feature_vector)
    return np.array(features)

# Detect anomalies in live traffic
def detect_anomalies(interface, model):
    def packet_callback(pkt):
        feature = extract_features([pkt])
        prediction = model.predict(feature)

        if prediction == -1:  # Anomaly detected
            print(f"[ALERT] Anomalous packet detected: {pkt.summary()}")
            log_security_event(pkt)

    sniff(iface=interface, prn=packet_callback, store=False)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Train on baseline traffic
    model = train_model("baseline_traffic.pcap")

    # Monitor live traffic
    detect_anomalies("eth0", model)
```

### Secure Gateway Implementation

**Gateway Security Functions**
1. **Traffic filtering** (firewall rules per zone)
2. **Protocol translation** (CAN ↔ Ethernet with validation)
3. **Rate limiting** (prevent DoS)
4. **Authentication** (verify sender identity)
5. **Logging** (audit trail for forensics)

**Secure Gateway Code Example**

```c
/* secure_gateway.c - Zone controller gateway with security checks */
#include "CanIf.h"
#include "EthIf.h"
#include "Crypto.h"

#define MAX_MESSAGES_PER_SECOND  100

/* Message authentication using HMAC-SHA256 */
typedef struct {
    uint32_t message_id;
    uint8_t payload[128];
    uint16_t payload_len;
    uint8_t hmac[32];  /* SHA-256 HMAC */
} AuthenticatedMessage_t;

static uint8_t shared_key[32] = { /* Pre-shared key for HMAC */ };
static uint32_t message_counter[256] = {0};  /* Per-source rate limiting */

bool Gateway_VerifyMessage(const AuthenticatedMessage_t* msg) {
    /* Compute HMAC over message */
    uint8_t computed_hmac[32];
    Crypto_HMAC_SHA256(
        shared_key, sizeof(shared_key),
        msg->payload, msg->payload_len,
        computed_hmac
    );

    /* Compare with received HMAC */
    if (memcmp(computed_hmac, msg->hmac, 32) != 0) {
        LogSecurityEvent(SEC_EVENT_INVALID_HMAC, msg->message_id);
        return false;
    }

    return true;
}

bool Gateway_RateLimit(uint8_t source_id) {
    message_counter[source_id]++;

    /* Reset counter every second (called by 1s timer) */
    static uint32_t last_reset_time = 0;
    if (GetCurrentTimeMs() - last_reset_time >= 1000) {
        memset(message_counter, 0, sizeof(message_counter));
        last_reset_time = GetCurrentTimeMs();
    }

    /* Check rate limit */
    if (message_counter[source_id] > MAX_MESSAGES_PER_SECOND) {
        LogSecurityEvent(SEC_EVENT_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, source_id);
        return false;
    }

    return true;
}

void Gateway_ForwardMessage(uint8_t source_id, const AuthenticatedMessage_t* msg) {
    /* Rate limiting */
    if (!Gateway_RateLimit(source_id)) {
        return;  /* Drop message */
    }

    /* Message authentication */
    if (!Gateway_VerifyMessage(msg)) {
        return;  /* Drop message */
    }

    /* Firewall rule check (whitelist) */
    if (!IsMessageAllowed(source_id, msg->message_id)) {
        LogSecurityEvent(SEC_EVENT_FIREWALL_DROP, msg->message_id);
        return;
    }

    /* Forward to destination (CAN or Ethernet) */
    if (IsCanDestination(msg->message_id)) {
        ForwardToCan(msg);
    } else {
        ForwardToEthernet(msg);
    }
}
```

### ISO 21434 Threat Analysis

**TARA (Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment)**

```yaml
# TARA for Zonal Architecture - Example
asset:
  name: FC_Zone_Controller
  criticality: high
  safety_level: ASIL-D

threats:
  - id: THREAT-001
    name: CAN Message Injection
    description: Attacker injects spoofed CAN messages from compromised sensor
    attack_vector: Physical access to CAN bus
    impact:
      safety: catastrophic (can control brakes)
      financial: high
      privacy: none
    likelihood: possible
    risk_level: very_high
    mitigations:
      - Implement CAN SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication)
      - Use message authentication (CMAC)
      - Firewall: Drop CAN messages from untrusted sources

  - id: THREAT-002
    name: Ethernet DoS Attack
    description: Attacker floods Ethernet link, causing safety message loss
    attack_vector: Compromised telematics unit
    impact:
      safety: major (can delay brake commands)
      financial: low
      privacy: none
    likelihood: likely
    risk_level: high
    mitigations:
      - Implement rate limiting (token bucket)
      - Use TSN Time-Aware Shaper (priority queuing)
      - Deploy IDS to detect floods

  - id: THREAT-003
    name: Firmware Tampering
    description: Attacker replaces zone controller firmware with malicious code
    attack_vector: Physical access to diagnostic port
    impact:
      safety: catastrophic
      financial: high
      privacy: high
    likelihood: unlikely
    risk_level: high
    mitigations:
      - Secure boot with code signing
      - Hardware Security Module (HSM) for key storage
      - Firmware update authentication (OTA with X.509 certs)
```

### Deliverables

When implementing network security for zonal architectures, provide:
1. Threat model (TARA) per ISO 21434
2. MACsec configuration files (per zone link)
3. IPsec VPN configuration (vehicle ↔ cloud)
4. Firewall rules (nftables/iptables)
5. IDS signature rules (Suricata/Snort)
6. Anomaly detection model (ML-based)
7. Security audit logs (SIEM integration)
8. Penetration test report (VAPT findings)

skills.name: automotive-architecture-zonal-architecture-design
skills.title: Electrical Electronic Architecture
skills.description: Expert in designing next-generation zonal E/E architectures with zone controllers, domain consolidation, topology optimization, and cable harness reduction strategies.
skills.content:
## 适用场景
- Zone controller placement and sizing for optimal coverage
- Migration from domain ECU architecture to zonal architecture
- Cable harness reduction (20-30% weight savings)
- Power distribution topology for zonal design
- Topology design for 100BASE-T1/1000BASE-T1 Ethernet backbone
- Cost-benefit analysis for zonal architecture migration

## 相关标准
- ISO 26262 (Functional Safety)
- ISO 21434 (Cybersecurity)
- AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform
- IEEE 802.1 TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking)
- SAE J3061 (Cybersecurity Guidebook)

## 约束
- Zone controller placement must minimize cable length (< 2m for sensors)
- Ethernet backbone latency < 5ms end-to-end (p99)
- Power consumption per zone < 100W
- ASIL-D safety for critical zones (steering, braking)
- ISO 21434 cybersecurity (firewall in each zone)
- Backward compatibility with existing sensors during migration

## 推荐工具
- CAD software (CATIA, Creo) for zone placement
- E/E architecture tools (SystemDesk, PREEvision, Capital)
- Network simulation (CANoe, ETAS COSYM)
- AUTOSAR toolchain (Vector DaVinci, EB tresos)
- Cable routing tools (Siemens Capital Harness)

## 方法
## Zonal Architecture Design Expertise

You are an expert in designing next-generation vehicle zonal E/E architectures that consolidate domain ECUs into zone controllers, reducing cable weight by 20-30% and enabling Software-Defined Vehicle capabilities.

### Architecture Evolution

**Traditional Domain Architecture**
- Centralized domain ECUs (Powertrain, Chassis, Body, ADAS, Infotainment)
- Point-to-point CAN/LIN wiring to sensors/actuators
- 3-5 km total cable length in premium vehicles
- Cable harness weight: 50-70 kg

**Zonal Architecture**
- 4-8 zone controllers placed geographically in vehicle
- Local aggregation of sensors/actuators per zone
- Ethernet backbone (TSN/AVB) connecting zones to central compute
- Cable harness weight: 30-50 kg (30% reduction)
- Gateway functions distributed to zone controllers

### Zone Controller Placement Strategy

**Typical Zonal Topology (7-zone example)**

1. **Front Left Zone (FL)**
   - Coverage: Front left corner, left headlight, left wheel
   - I/O: 40-60 signals (headlight control, turn signals, wheel speed, brake pressure)
   - Compute: NXP S32K344 or Renesas RH850/U2A
   - Power: 12V switched, 5V/3.3V local regulation

2. **Front Center Zone (FC)**
   - Coverage: Front bumper, grille, ADAS sensors
   - I/O: 50-80 signals (radar, camera, lidar, ultrasonic sensors)
   - Compute: NXP S32G3 (gateway + ADAS aggregation)
   - Power: 12V continuous, 5V/3.3V, battery backup for ADAS

3. **Front Right Zone (FR)**
   - Coverage: Front right corner, right headlight, right wheel
   - I/O: 40-60 signals (symmetric to FL)
   - Compute: NXP S32K344 or Renesas RH850/U2A
   - Power: 12V switched, 5V/3.3V local regulation

4. **Central Zone (C)**
   - Coverage: Dashboard, center console, HVAC
   - I/O: 80-120 signals (display, switches, climate control)
   - Compute: Infineon AURIX TC3xx or NXP S32G3
   - Power: 12V continuous, multiple voltage rails

5. **Rear Left Zone (RL)**
   - Coverage: Left rear door, left rear wheel, left tail light
   - I/O: 40-60 signals (door locks, windows, lighting, wheel speed)
   - Compute: NXP S32K344
   - Power: 12V switched, 5V/3.3V local regulation

6. **Rear Center Zone (RC)**
   - Coverage: Trunk, rear bumper, backup sensors
   - I/O: 30-50 signals (trunk actuators, parking sensors, rear camera)
   - Compute: NXP S32K344
   - Power: 12V switched, 5V/3.3V local regulation

7. **Rear Right Zone (RR)**
   - Coverage: Right rear door, right rear wheel, right tail light
   - I/O: 40-60 signals (symmetric to RL)
   - Compute: NXP S32K344
   - Power: 12V switched, 5V/3.3V local regulation

**Central Compute Platform**
- High-performance SoC (NVIDIA Orin, Qualcomm Snapdragon Ride, NXP S32G399A)
- 100+ TOPS AI compute for ADAS/AD
- Connected to all zone controllers via Ethernet TSN
- Runs AUTOSAR Adaptive or Linux-based middleware

### Cable Harness Reduction

**Traditional Architecture**
```
Total cable length: 4,500 meters
- Front headlight → Body ECU: 6 meters × 2 = 12m
- Wheel speed sensors → Chassis ECU: 5m × 4 = 20m
- Door switches → Body ECU: 8m × 4 = 32m
- Tail lights → Body ECU: 10m × 2 = 20m
- ADAS sensors → ADAS ECU: 15m × 5 = 75m
... (hundreds more connections)
```

**Zonal Architecture**
```
Total cable length: 3,200 meters (29% reduction)
- Front headlight → FC zone controller: 0.5m × 2 = 1m
- Wheel speed sensors → corner zone: 0.8m × 4 = 3.2m
- Door switches → door zone: 0.3m × 4 = 1.2m
- Tail lights → RC zone: 0.5m × 2 = 1m
- ADAS sensors → FC zone: 1m × 5 = 5m
- Ethernet backbone (7 zones): 25m total
```

**Weight Savings**
- Cable weight reduction: 15-20 kg
- Connector count reduction: 30-40%
- Assembly time reduction: 20%
- Cost savings: $200-300 per vehicle (offset by zone controller cost)

### Network Topology Design

**Star Topology (Recommended for Safety)**
```
Central Compute
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ FL Zone
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ FC Zone (with TSN switch for ADAS)
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ FR Zone
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ C Zone
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ RL Zone
  ├─ 100BASE-T1 ─ RC Zone
  └─ 100BASE-T1 ─ RR Zone
```
- Bandwidth: 100 Mbps per zone (sufficient for sensor aggregation)
- Latency: < 2ms end-to-end (single hop)
- Fault isolation: Zone failure doesn't cascade

**Daisy Chain Topology (Cost-optimized)**
```
Central Compute ─ FL ─ FC ─ FR ─ C ─ RL ─ RC ─ RR
```
- Lower cost (fewer Ethernet PHYs in central compute)
- Higher latency (multi-hop, up to 5ms)
- Single point of failure risk

**Ring Topology with TSN (High Availability)**
```
     Central Compute
        /        \
      FL ─ FC ─ FR
      |           |
      C           RR
      |           |
     RL ─ RC ─ (back to Central)
```
- Redundant paths for critical data
- TSN time-aware shaper for deterministic latency
- Used in ADAS/AD vehicles (Tesla, VW.OS)

### Ethernet Physical Layer

**100BASE-T1 (IEEE 802.3bw)**
- Bandwidth: 100 Mbps full-duplex
- Cable: Single twisted pair (STP or UTP)
- Max length: 15 meters (40 meters with active repeater)
- Power: < 1W per port
- Use case: Zone controller to central compute

**1000BASE-T1 (IEEE 802.3bp)**
- Bandwidth: 1 Gbps full-duplex
- Cable: Single twisted pair
- Max length: 15 meters (40 meters with active repeater)
- Power: 1-2W per port
- Use case: High-bandwidth zones (FC with cameras), central to TSN switch

**10BASE-T1S (IEEE 802.3cg)**
- Bandwidth: 10 Mbps (multidrop bus)
- Cable: Shared twisted pair (up to 8 nodes)
- Max length: 25 meters per segment
- Use case: Low-cost sensors (door switches, climate sensors)

### Power Distribution Architecture

**Traditional Architecture**
- Central power distribution box (fuse box)
- Heavy gauge wires to high-current loads
- Multiple fuse blocks

**Zonal Power Distribution**
```
Battery ─ Main Power Distribution
  ├─ FL Zone PDU (Power Distribution Unit)
  │   ├─ 12V switched (headlights, motors)
  │   ├─ 12V continuous (zone controller)
  │   └─ 5V/3.3V regulation for sensors
  ├─ FC Zone PDU
  │   ├─ 12V continuous (ADAS sensors)
  │   ├─ Battery backup (5Ah for parking mode)
  │   └─ 5V/3.3V for cameras/radar
  ├─ Central Zone PDU
  │   ├─ 12V continuous (infotainment, HVAC)
  │   └─ 48V (for HVAC compressor, optional)
  └─ ... (other zones)
```

**Benefits**
- Local fusing reduces wire gauge (thinner cables)
- Intelligent load management per zone
- Soft-start for inductive loads (reduces inrush current)
- Diagnostic capability (current sensing per channel)

### Zone Controller Hardware Selection

**NXP S32K344 (Low-cost Zone)**
- CPU: Arm Cortex-M7 @ 160 MHz
- I/O: 144 GPIO, 16 CAN-FD, 6 LIN, 2 Ethernet
- Memory: 4 MB Flash, 512 KB RAM
- Safety: ASIL-B out-of-box, ASIL-D with lockstep
- Cost: $15-20 per unit
- Use case: Corner zones (FL, FR, RL, RR)

**Renesas RH850/U2A (Mid-range Zone)**
- CPU: RH850 G4MH @ 320 MHz
- I/O: 256 GPIO, 12 CAN-FD, 8 LIN, 1 Gigabit Ethernet
- Memory: 8 MB Flash, 1 MB RAM
- Safety: ASIL-D certified
- Cost: $25-35 per unit
- Use case: Central zone, FC zone (without ADAS)

**NXP S32G274A (Gateway Zone)**
- CPU: 4× Arm Cortex-A53 @ 1 GHz + 3× Cortex-M7 @ 400 MHz
- I/O: 16 CAN-FD, 4× Gigabit Ethernet with TSN
- Memory: 16 MB internal + external DDR4
- Safety: ASIL-D on M7 cores
- Cost: $80-120 per unit
- Use case: FC zone with ADAS gateway, or standalone central gateway

**Infineon AURIX TC397 (High-performance Zone)**
- CPU: 3× TriCore 1.8 GHz
- I/O: 20 CAN-FD, 8 LIN, 2 Gigabit Ethernet
- Memory: 16 MB Flash, 6 MB RAM
- Safety: ASIL-D with lockstep and ECC
- Cost: $60-90 per unit
- Use case: Central zone with complex body control logic

### Migration Strategy from Domain to Zonal

**Phase 1: Hybrid Architecture (2-3 years)**
- Keep existing domain ECUs
- Add 2-3 zone controllers for new sensors (ADAS, V2X)
- Ethernet backbone connects domains + zones
- Example: VW MEB platform (ID.3, ID.4)

**Phase 2: Domain Consolidation (3-5 years)**
- Merge Body + Comfort into Central Zone
- Merge Powertrain + Chassis into Front Center Zone (if FWD)
- ADAS remains separate but connected to FC zone
- Example: Tesla Model 3/Y (5 domains → 3 zones)

**Phase 3: Full Zonal (5+ years)**
- 6-8 geographic zones
- Central compute for ADAS/AD + cloud connectivity
- All domain functions distributed to zones
- Example: VW.OS (Cariad Trinity), GM Ultifi

### Example ARXML Zone Definition (AUTOSAR Adaptive)

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<AUTOSAR xmlns="http://autosar.org/schema/r4.0">
  <AR-PACKAGES>
    <AR-PACKAGE>
      <SHORT-NAME>ZonalArchitecture</SHORT-NAME>
      <ELEMENTS>
        <!-- Front Center Zone Controller -->
        <ECU-INSTANCE>
          <SHORT-NAME>FC_ZoneController</SHORT-NAME>
          <COMM-CONTROLLERS>
            <!-- Ethernet to Central Compute -->
            <ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER>
              <SHORT-NAME>Eth_CentralCompute</SHORT-NAME>
              <ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-VARIANTS>
                <ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-CONDITIONAL>
                  <MAC-UNICAST-ADDRESS>02:00:00:00:00:01</MAC-UNICAST-ADDRESS>
                  <MAXIMUM-TRANSMISSION-UNIT>1500</MAXIMUM-TRANSMISSION-UNIT>
                </ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-CONDITIONAL>
              </ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-VARIANTS>
            </ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER>
            <!-- CAN-FD for local sensors -->
            <CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER>
              <SHORT-NAME>Can_LocalSensors</SHORT-NAME>
              <CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-VARIANTS>
                <CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-CONDITIONAL>
                  <CAN-CONTROLLER-FD-ATTRIBUTES>
                    <CAN-FD-BAUDRATE>2000000</CAN-FD-BAUDRATE>
                  </CAN-CONTROLLER-FD-ATTRIBUTES>
                </CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-CONDITIONAL>
              </CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER-VARIANTS>
            </CAN-COMMUNICATION-CONTROLLER>
          </COMM-CONTROLLERS>
          <CONNECTORS>
            <COMMUNICATION-CONNECTOR-REF-CONDITIONAL>
              <COMMUNICATION-CONNECTOR-REF DEST="ETHERNET-COMMUNICATION-CONNECTOR">/System/Topology/FC_Eth0</COMMUNICATION-CONNECTOR-REF>
            </COMMUNICATION-CONNECTOR-REF-CONDITIONAL>
          </CONNECTORS>
        </ECU-INSTANCE>

        <!-- Zone I/O Configuration -->
        <HARDWARE-DESCRIPTION>
          <SHORT-NAME>FC_Zone_Hardware</SHORT-NAME>
          <HW-ELEMENT>
            <SHORT-NAME>FrontRadar</SHORT-NAME>
            <HW-CATEGORY>SENSOR</HW-CATEGORY>
            <HW-PIN-GROUPS>
              <HW-PIN-GROUP>
                <SHORT-NAME>CAN_Interface</SHORT-NAME>
                <HW-PINS>
                  <HW-PIN>
                    <SHORT-NAME>CAN_H</SHORT-NAME>
                  </HW-PIN>
                  <HW-PIN>
                    <SHORT-NAME>CAN_L</SHORT-NAME>
                  </HW-PIN>
                </HW-PINS>
              </HW-PIN-GROUP>
            </HW-PIN-GROUPS>
          </HW-ELEMENT>
          <HW-ELEMENT>
            <SHORT-NAME>FrontCamera</SHORT-NAME>
            <HW-CATEGORY>SENSOR</HW-CATEGORY>
            <HW-PIN-GROUPS>
              <HW-PIN-GROUP>
                <SHORT-NAME>MIPI_CSI2</SHORT-NAME>
                <!-- High-speed camera interface -->
              </HW-PIN-GROUP>
            </HW-PIN-GROUPS>
          </HW-ELEMENT>
        </HARDWARE-DESCRIPTION>
      </ELEMENTS>
    </AR-PACKAGE>
  </AR-PACKAGES>
</AUTOSAR>
```

### Zone Controller Network Configuration YAML

```yaml
# FC Zone Controller - Front Center Zone
zone_controller:
  id: fc_zone
  name: Front Center Zone Controller
  hardware:
    platform: NXP_S32G274A
    cpu_cores:
      - type: Cortex-A53
        count: 4
        frequency_mhz: 1000
      - type: Cortex-M7
        count: 3
        frequency_mhz: 400
    memory:
      flash_mb: 16
      ram_mb: 2048  # 2GB DDR4
      eeprom_kb: 256

  network_interfaces:
    - name: eth0
      type: 100BASE-T1
      speed_mbps: 100
      mac: "02:00:00:00:00:01"
      vlan_support: true
      tsn_enabled: true
      connected_to: central_compute
      ip_address: 192.168.10.10/24

    - name: can0
      type: CAN-FD
      baudrate_kbps: 500
      data_baudrate_kbps: 2000
      connected_devices:
        - front_radar_left
        - front_radar_right
        - ultrasonic_sensors_front

    - name: can1
      type: CAN-FD
      baudrate_kbps: 500
      data_baudrate_kbps: 2000
      connected_devices:
        - front_camera_left
        - front_camera_center
        - front_camera_right

  local_io:
    digital_inputs: 32
    digital_outputs: 24
    analog_inputs: 8
    pwm_channels: 12
    lin_channels: 4

  power:
    input_voltage: 12V
    input_current_max: 15A
    power_consumption_typical: 30W
    power_consumption_max: 80W
    voltage_regulators:
      - output: 5V
        current_max: 5A
        use: sensors
      - output: 3.3V
        current_max: 3A
        use: logic

  safety:
    asil_level: ASIL-D
    watchdog: external
    ecc_memory: true
    dual_core_lockstep: true
    memory_protection_unit: true

  connected_sensors:
    - name: front_radar_left
      type: radar
      protocol: CAN-FD
      message_rate_hz: 20
      data_size_bytes: 64

    - name: front_camera_center
      type: camera
      protocol: MIPI-CSI2
      resolution: 1920x1080
      fps: 30
      bandwidth_mbps: 50

  software:
    operating_system: AUTOSAR_Adaptive_R23-11
    middleware:
      - SOME/IP
      - DDS
    services:
      - sensor_aggregation
      - gateway_routing
      - diagnostic_logging
```

### Cost-Benefit Analysis

**Traditional Domain Architecture (7 ECUs)**
- ECU cost: 7 × $80 = $560
- Cable harness: $450
- Assembly: $200
- **Total: $1,210**

**Zonal Architecture (7 Zone Controllers + 1 Central Compute)**
- Zone controllers: 4 × $20 (corners) + 2 × $30 (rear/central) + 1 × $100 (FC with gateway) = $280
- Central compute: $350 (high-performance SoC)
- Cable harness: $320 (29% reduction)
- Assembly: $150 (25% reduction due to fewer connectors)
- **Total: $1,100**
- **Savings: $110 per vehicle**

**Non-monetary Benefits**
- 15-20 kg weight reduction (improves fuel economy / EV range)
- Simplified assembly (20% faster harness installation)
- Over-the-air update capability (Software-Defined Vehicle)
- Future-proof for ADAS/AD scaling

### Reference Architectures

**Tesla Model 3/Y (Simplified Zonal)**
- Central compute: FSD Computer (144 TOPS)
- Left body controller (door, seats, windows)
- Right body controller (symmetric)
- Front power distribution
- Rear power distribution

**VW.OS (Full Zonal - 2025+)**
- 6 zone controllers (FL, FC, FR, RL, RC, RR)
- Central compute: 2× ADAS ECU (NVIDIA Orin)
- TSN Ethernet backbone (1 Gbps ring)
- AUTOSAR Adaptive on all zones

**GM Ultifi (Service-Oriented Zonal)**
- 5 zone controllers
- Central middleware (DDS-based)
- SOME/IP for service discovery
- Linux-based zone software

### Deliverables

When designing zonal architectures, provide:
1. Zone placement diagram with coverage area
2. Cable harness comparison (before/after)
3. Bill of Materials (BOM) with part numbers
4. Network topology diagram (Ethernet + CAN/LIN)
5. Power distribution schematic per zone
6. ARXML configuration for zone ECUs
7. Migration roadmap (domain → zonal)
8. Cost-benefit analysis with ROI timeline

skills.name: automotive-autosar-adaptive-ara-com
skills.title: Ara Com
skills.description: Skills for AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform service-oriented communication
skills.content:
## 方法
## AUTOSAR Adaptive ara::com Communication Guide

### Overview

ara::com is the communication middleware API of the AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform,
enabling service-oriented communication between Adaptive Applications (AA).
It abstracts the underlying transport (SOME/IP, DDS, IPC) and provides a
type-safe C++ API for methods, events, and fields.

### Architecture

```
Adaptive Application A                    Adaptive Application B
┌─────────────────────┐                  ┌─────────────────────┐
│  Proxy (Consumer)   │ ◄──────────────► │  Skeleton (Provider) │
│  - FindService()    │   SOME/IP or DDS │  - OfferService()    │
│  - Subscribe()      │                  │  - Send()            │
│  - Call()           │                  │  - Fire()            │
└─────────────────────┘                  └─────────────────────┘
```

### Service Interface Definition (ARXML)

Every ara::com service starts with an ARXML service interface definition
that specifies methods, events, and fields. The toolchain generates C++
proxy and skeleton classes from this definition.

Key elements in the ServiceInterface ARXML:
- **Methods**: Request-response operations with typed arguments
- **Events**: Publish-subscribe notifications with typed payloads
- **Fields**: Combination of notifier, getter, and setter
- **ApplicationErrors**: Typed error returns from methods

### Service Discovery

Service discovery uses SOME/IP-SD (Service Discovery) protocol or DDS
discovery to find service instances on the network at runtime.

**FindService patterns**:
- `StartFindService()` with callback: Asynchronous, recommended for production
- `FindService()` blocking: Synchronous, useful for initialization
- Both return `ServiceHandleContainer` with matched instances

**Service instance manifest** defines:
- Service ID and instance ID mappings
- Transport binding (SOME/IP, IPC, DDS)
- Network endpoint (IP, port, protocol)
- Event group assignments

### Proxy (Client) Side

The proxy class is generated from the service interface and provides:

```cpp
// Find and use a service
auto handles = proxy::RadarServiceProxy::FindService(instanceSpec);
auto proxy = std::make_unique<proxy::RadarServiceProxy>(handles[0]);

// Subscribe to events
proxy->BrakeEvent.Subscribe(10);  // max 10 samples in cache
proxy->BrakeEvent.SetReceiveHandler([&]() {
    proxy->BrakeEvent.GetNewSamples([](auto sample) {
        ProcessBrakeData(*sample);
    });
});

// Call methods (returns ara::core::Future)
auto future = proxy->Calibrate(sensorId, params);
auto result = future.get();  // Blocking wait
```

### Skeleton (Server) Side

The skeleton class is generated and must be subclassed:

```cpp
class RadarServiceImpl : public skeleton::RadarServiceSkeleton {
public:
    RadarServiceImpl(ara::core::InstanceSpecifier spec)
        : RadarServiceSkeleton(spec) {}

    // Implement method handlers
    ara::core::Future<CalibrationOutput> Calibrate(
        uint32_t sensorId, CalibrationParams params) override {
        ara::core::Promise<CalibrationOutput> promise;
        // Process calibration
        CalibrationOutput result{true, 0.98};
        promise.set_value(result);
        return promise.get_future();
    }

    // Send events
    void SendBrakeEvent(const BrakeEventData& data) {
        BrakeEvent.Send(data);
    }
};
```

### Event Communication

Events follow publish-subscribe semantics:
- **Publisher** allocates sample, fills data, calls `Send()`
- **Subscriber** calls `Subscribe()`, sets receive handler, processes samples
- Subscription states: kSubscribed, kNotSubscribed, kSubscriptionPending
- Max sample count limits memory usage on subscriber side

### Field Communication

Fields combine getter, setter, and notifier:
- **Getter**: On-demand read of current value
- **Setter**: Write a new value
- **Notifier**: Automatic notification on value change
- Fields always have an initial value available after subscription

### SOME/IP Binding Configuration

SOME/IP is the primary transport for ara::com in automotive:

| Parameter | Typical Value | Description |
|-----------|--------------|-------------|
| Service ID | 0x0001-0xFFFE | Unique per service type |
| Instance ID | 0x0001-0xFFFE | Unique per service instance |
| Method ID | 0x0001-0x7FFF | Per-method identifier |
| Event ID | 0x8001-0xFFFE | Per-event identifier |
| Event Group | 0x0001-0xFFFE | Group events for subscription |

Transport options:
- **UDP**: Low latency, no connection overhead, for events
- **TCP**: Reliable delivery, for methods and large payloads
- **Local IPC**: Shared memory for same-ECU communication

### Serialization

SOME/IP serialization supports:
- TLV (Tag-Length-Value): Flexible, backward compatible
- Length-delimited: For variable-length fields
- Fixed-length: For primitive types
- Byte order: Big-endian (network byte order)

### Error Handling

ara::com uses typed errors and exceptions:
- `ara::com::ComErrc`: Communication-level errors
- `ApplicationError`: Service-defined error codes
- `ara::core::Future` with `GetResult()` returns `Result<T, E>`
- Handle `ComOfferServiceErrc` for service offering failures

### Thread Safety

- Proxy and skeleton methods are thread-safe by default
- Event receive handlers execute in middleware context (not application thread)
- Use `ara::core::Promise` for asynchronous method returns
- Avoid blocking in receive handlers; queue work for processing threads

### Testing and Debugging

- Use SOME/IP dissector in Wireshark for protocol analysis
- vsomeip logging (VSOMEIP_LOGLEVEL) for middleware tracing
- Mock services using test skeletons for unit testing
- Validate service discovery with SOME/IP-SD packet captures

### Best Practices

- Define clear service interfaces with versioning strategy
- Use event groups to minimize network traffic (subscribe only needed events)
- Set appropriate max sample counts to bound memory usage
- Handle service availability changes (gone/available transitions)
- Use `ara::core::Future::then()` for non-blocking method chains
- Keep method handler execution short; offload heavy work to threads
- Test with network delays and packet loss for robustness
- Version service interfaces for backward compatibility

skills.name: automotive-autosar-swc-generation
skills.title: Swc Generation
skills.description: Comprehensive skills for AUTOSAR Classic Software Component generation and configuration
skills.content:
## 方法
## AUTOSAR Classic Platform SWC Development Guide

### Overview

AUTOSAR Classic Platform defines a layered software architecture for embedded
automotive ECUs. Software Components (SWCs) are the application-level building
blocks that communicate through the Runtime Environment (RTE). This guide covers
SWC creation, BSW configuration, RTE generation, and integration.

### Architecture

```
Application Layer
┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
│  App SWC │  │ Sensor   │  │ Actuator │
│          │  │ Actuator │  │ SWC      │
│          │  │ SWC      │  │          │
└────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
     │              │              │
─────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴────── RTE
     │              │              │
┌────┴─────┐  ┌────┴─────┐  ┌────┴─────┐
│  Com     │  │  OS      │  │  DEM     │
│  Stack   │  │  (SchM)  │  │  NvM     │
└──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
Basic Software (BSW)
```

### SWC Types

- **ApplicationSWC**: Standard application logic (e.g., control algorithms)
- **SensorActuatorSWC**: Direct hardware I/O access (sensor reading, actuator driving)
- **ComplexDeviceDriverSWC**: Bypass BSW for special hardware
- **ParameterSWC**: Calibration parameter storage
- **CompositionSWC**: Groups multiple SWCs into a single unit

### Port Interface Types

**Sender-Receiver (SR) Interface**:
- Asynchronous data exchange between SWCs
- Supports queued or last-is-best semantics
- Data elements defined with application data types
- Init values required for startup safety

**Client-Server (CS) Interface**:
- Synchronous request-response operations
- Client calls operation, server executes and returns result
- Supports typed error responses (ApplicationErrors)
- Can be synchronous or asynchronous

### Runnable Entity Configuration

Runnables are the execution units within an SWC. Each runnable maps to a C function:
- **TimingEvent**: Periodic execution (e.g., every 10ms)
- **DataReceivedEvent**: Triggered when new data arrives on an SR port
- **OperationInvokedEvent**: Triggered when a CS operation is called
- **ModeSwitchEvent**: Triggered on mode transitions

Key properties per runnable:
- Minimum start interval (prevents re-entry)
- Data access points (read/write permissions)
- Exclusive area usage for mutual exclusion
- Inter-runnable variable access

### RTE API Patterns

```c
/* Sender-Receiver Read */
Std_ReturnType ret;
SpeedType speed;
ret = Rte_Read_RpSpeed_Speed(&speed);
if (ret == RTE_E_OK) { /* use speed */ }

/* Sender-Receiver Write */
Rte_Write_PpTorque_TorqueRequest(requestedTorque);

/* Client-Server Call */
CalibResult result;
ret = Rte_Call_RpCalibrate_Calibrate(sensorId, &result);

/* Inter-Runnable Variable */
uint16 filteredValue = Rte_IrvRead_Runnable10ms_FilteredSignal();
Rte_IrvWrite_Runnable10ms_FilteredSignal(newValue);

/* Exclusive Area */
Rte_Enter_ExclusiveArea_0();
/* critical section */
Rte_Exit_ExclusiveArea_0();
```

### BSW Module Stack Configuration

**CAN Communication Stack** (bottom to top):
1. Can Driver (CanDrv) - Hardware register access
2. CAN Interface (CanIf) - Abstraction, HOH mapping
3. CAN Transport Protocol (CanTp) - Segmented transfers
4. PDU Router (PduR) - Routes PDUs between modules
5. COM module - Signal-level access for application

**Memory Stack**:
1. Flash Driver (Fls) - Raw flash operations
2. Flash EEPROM Emulation (Fee) - Block-based abstraction
3. NV RAM Manager (NvM) - Application-level persistent data

**Diagnostic Stack**:
1. CAN Transport (CanTp) - UDS transport
2. Diagnostic Communication Manager (DCM) - UDS services
3. Diagnostic Event Manager (DEM) - Fault memory

### AUTOSAR OS Configuration

- Tasks with fixed priorities (OSEK/VDX-based)
- Events for synchronization between tasks
- Alarms for periodic task activation
- Resources for mutual exclusion (ceiling protocol)
- ISR Category 1 (no OS calls) and Category 2 (OS calls allowed)
- Application partitions for memory protection (ISO 26262)

### Safety Mechanisms

**End-to-End Protection (E2E)**:
- Profile 1: CRC-8 + counter (4-byte overhead)
- Profile 2: CRC-8 + counter + data ID (4-byte)
- Profile 4: CRC-32 + counter + data ID (12-byte)
- Profile 11: CRC-8 + counter (compact)
- Configured per signal or signal group

**Watchdog Supervision (SafeWdgM)**:
- Alive supervision: Checks periodic execution
- Deadline supervision: Checks execution time
- Logical supervision: Checks control flow sequence
- Reports to DEM on supervision failures

### Secure Onboard Communication (SecOC)

- CMAC authentication for CAN messages
- Freshness value management (counter or timestamp)
- Configured per PDU (not per signal)
- Key management through Crypto Service Manager (CSM)

### Code Generation and Validation

1. Define service interfaces and SWCs in ARXML
2. Configure BSW modules (EB tresos, DaVinci Configurator)
3. Generate RTE code (Rte.h, Rte_<SWC>.h, Rte.c)
4. Implement SWC runnables using generated API
5. Generate BSW configuration code
6. Compile and link complete ECU software
7. Validate with MISRA-C checker and static analysis

### Testing Strategy

- **Unit Test**: Mock RTE with stubs, test runnable logic in isolation
- **Integration Test**: CANoe/dSPACE for signal-level validation
- **System Test**: Hardware-in-the-loop with real ECU
- **Regression**: Automated test suite run on every build

### Best Practices

- Keep runnables short (< 50 lines) and focused on one responsibility
- Use exclusive areas sparingly; prefer data flow over shared state
- Define clear init values for all SR data elements
- Version your ARXML files alongside source code
- Validate ARXML consistency before RTE generation
- Document the mapping between SWC ports and CAN signals
- Use calibration parameters (not constants) for tunable values
- Configure E2E protection for all safety-critical signals

## 适用场景
- AUTOSAR system development
- Diagnostic Stack optimization
- Production ECU implementation

## 相关标准
- ISO 26262
- ASPICE Level 3
- AUTOSAR 4.4
- ISO 21434

## 约束
- ISO 26262 functional safety compliance
- Real-time performance requirements
- Resource constraints (CPU/Memory)
- AUTOSAR architecture adherence

## 推荐工具
- MATLAB/Simulink
- Vector CANoe/CANalyzer
- Static analyzer (Polyspace/Klocwork)
- AUTOSAR toolchain

## 方法
## Core Competencies

Expert in diagnostic stack for automotive autosar systems.

## Approach

1. Analyze requirements against automotive standards
2. Design solution following AUTOSAR patterns
3. Implement with safety and security considerations
4. Validate per ISO 26262 requirements

## Deliverables

- Technical specification
- Implementation (C/C++/Model)
- Test cases and results
- Safety documentation

## 适用场景
- AUTOSAR system development
- Nm Stack optimization
- Production ECU implementation

## 相关标准
- ISO 26262
- ASPICE Level 3
- AUTOSAR 4.4
- ISO 21434

## 约束
- ISO 26262 functional safety compliance
- Real-time performance requirements
- Resource constraints (CPU/Memory)
- AUTOSAR architecture adherence

## 推荐工具
- MATLAB/Simulink
- Vector CANoe/CANalyzer
- Static analyzer (Polyspace/Klocwork)
- AUTOSAR toolchain

## 方法
## Core Competencies

Expert in nm stack for automotive autosar systems.

## Approach

1. Analyze requirements against automotive standards
2. Design solution following AUTOSAR patterns
3. Implement with safety and security considerations
4. Validate per ISO 26262 requirements

## Deliverables

- Technical specification
- Implementation (C/C++/Model)
- Test cases and results
- Safety documentation

## 适用场景
- AUTOSAR system development
- Rte optimization
- Production ECU implementation

## 相关标准
- ISO 26262
- ASPICE Level 3
- AUTOSAR 4.4
- ISO 21434

## 约束
- ISO 26262 functional safety compliance
- Real-time performance requirements
- Resource constraints (CPU/Memory)
- AUTOSAR architecture adherence

## 推荐工具
- MATLAB/Simulink
- Vector CANoe/CANalyzer
- Static analyzer (Polyspace/Klocwork)
- AUTOSAR toolchain

## 方法
## Core Competencies

Expert in rte for automotive autosar systems.

## Approach

1. Analyze requirements against automotive standards
2. Design solution following AUTOSAR patterns
3. Implement with safety and security considerations
4. Validate per ISO 26262 requirements

## Deliverables

- Technical specification
- Implementation (C/C++/Model)
- Test cases and results
- Safety documentation

skills.name: automotive-battery-bms-cell-balancing
skills.title: Cell Balancing
skills.description: Active and passive cell balancing strategies for battery pack voltage equalization
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement cell balancing for battery packs:

Passive balancing:
- Dissipative balancing with resistors
- Simple and low cost
- Energy wasted as heat (inefficient)
- Typical: 100-500 mA balancing current

Active balancing:
- Capacitor-based charge shuttling
- Inductor-based energy transfer
- Transformer-based pack-to-cell
- More efficient but complex and costly
- Typical: 1-5 A balancing current

Balancing strategies:
- Top balancing (during charge at high SOC)
- Bottom balancing (during discharge at low SOC)
- Continuous balancing (during operation)

Implementation:
- Monitor cell voltages continuously
- Calculate voltage differences
- Activate balancing when ΔV > threshold
- Prioritize cells with highest deviation
- Stop balancing when ΔV < target

Performance targets:
- Voltage uniformity: ΔV < 50 mV
- Balancing time: < 2 hours for full balance
- Energy efficiency: > 90% for active balancing

skills.name: automotive-battery-bms-soc-estimation
skills.title: Soc Estimation
skills.description: State of Charge (SOC) estimation using Coulomb counting, Kalman filtering, and machine learning approaches
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement SOC estimation algorithms for battery management systems:

Coulomb counting:
- Integrate current over time
- Account for charge/discharge efficiency
- Compensate for self-discharge
- Accumulate errors over time (drift)

Kalman Filter-based:
- Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) with battery model
- Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for nonlinear dynamics
- Fuse voltage, current, temperature measurements
- More accurate than pure coulomb counting

Machine Learning:
- Neural networks trained on cycling data
- LSTM for temporal patterns
- Feature engineering (voltage, current, temp, internal resistance)
- Requires extensive training data

Battery models:
- Equivalent Circuit Models (ECM): Thevenin, PNGV
- Electrochemical models: Single Particle Model (SPM)
- Empirical models: polynomial voltage-SOC curves

Performance requirements:
- Accuracy: ±2% for EKF, ±5% for coulomb counting
- Update rate: 1-10 Hz
- Temperature range: -20°C to 60°C
- Converge within 5 minutes of operation

skills.name: automotive-battery-bms-soh-prediction
skills.title: Soh Prediction
skills.description: State of Health (SOH) prediction using capacity fade models, cycle counting, and machine learning
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement SOH estimation and prediction for battery aging management:

Capacity fade models:
- Semi-empirical aging models (power-law, exponential)
- Calendar aging: temperature and SOC dependent
- Cycle aging: depth of discharge (DOD) and C-rate dependent
- Combined stress factors

Cycle counting:
- Rainflow counting algorithm for irregular cycles
- Equivalent full cycles (EFC) calculation
- Weighted damage accumulation

Machine learning:
- Feature extraction from cycling data
- LSTM/GRU for temporal degradation patterns
- Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction
- Transfer learning across different cell chemistries

Health indicators:
- Capacity: Q_current / Q_nominal
- Internal resistance increase
- Power fade
- Energy fade

Targets:
- SOH accuracy: ±3%
- RUL prediction: ±10% error at 80% SOH
- Update frequency: daily or per charge cycle

skills.name: automotive-battery-charging-ccs-protocol
skills.title: Ccs Protocol
skills.description: Combined Charging System (CCS) protocol implementation for DC fast charging with ISO 15118 communication
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement CCS charging protocol stack:

Protocol layers:
- Physical: PLC (Power Line Communication) HPGP
- Data Link: IEEE 1901
- Network: IPv6
- Transport: TCP/UDP
- Application: ISO 15118-2/20

Charging phases:
1. Plugin detection and wake-up
2. Communication setup (SLAC)
3. Authentication and authorization
4. Charge parameter discovery
5. Cable check and pre-charge
6. Power delivery (CV/CC control)
7. Welding check and disconnect

Power profiles:
- CCS Combo 1 (Type 1): up to 350 kW
- CCS Combo 2 (Type 2): up to 350 kW
- Voltage: 200-920V DC
- Current: up to 500A

Safety requirements:
- Isolation monitoring
- Ground fault detection
- Overcurrent protection
- Temperature monitoring
- Emergency stop handling

skills.name: automotive-ev-motor-control-foc-control
skills.title: Foc Control
skills.description: Field-Oriented Control (FOC) for PMSM/BLDC motors with space vector modulation and sensorless operation
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement Field-Oriented Control (FOC) for EV traction motors:

Control architecture:
- Clarke transform (abc → αβ)
- Park transform (αβ → dq rotating frame)
- PI controllers for Id and Iq currents
- Inverse Park transform (dq → αβ)
- Space Vector Modulation (SVM)

Feedback requirements:
- Phase currents (Ia, Ib, Ic)
- Rotor position (encoder or sensorless estimation)
- DC bus voltage

Sensorless operation:
- Back-EMF observer
- Sliding mode observer
- High-frequency injection (low speed)

Performance targets:
- Current control bandwidth: 1-2 kHz
- Torque ripple: < 3%
- Efficiency: > 95% at rated load
- Maximum speed: 15,000 RPM

skills.name: automotive-ev-motor-control-regenerative-braking
skills.title: Regenerative Braking
skills.description: Regenerative braking control for energy recovery and range extension in EVs
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement regenerative braking system:

Control strategy:
- Blend regenerative and friction braking
- Maximize energy recovery (up to 70% in urban)
- Ensure driver feel and safety
- Coordinate with ABS/ESC

Braking regions:
- Light braking: 100% regenerative
- Medium braking: blend regen + friction
- Heavy braking: mostly friction (safety)
- Emergency: full friction braking

Constraints:
- Motor speed limits (max regen at high RPM)
- Battery charge limits (SOC, current, power)
- Thermal limits (motor and battery)
- Traction limits (wheel slip)

Energy recovery:
- Urban driving: 15-30% range extension
- Highway: 5-10% range extension
- Capture deceleration kinetic energy

Implementation:
- Monitor brake pedal position
- Calculate available regen torque
- Coordinate with friction brake
- Limit regen based on battery SOC
- Smooth torque transitions

skills.name: automotive-battery-thermal-thermal-management
skills.title: Thermal Management
skills.description: Battery thermal management using liquid cooling, air cooling, and heat pipe systems with predictive control
skills.content:
## 方法
Implement battery thermal management strategies:

Cooling methods:
- Liquid cooling (most efficient, 30-40°C optimal range)
- Air cooling (simpler, 20-45°C range)
- Phase change materials (PCM) for peak absorption
- Heat pipes for uniform distribution

Control strategies:
- PID control for coolant temperature
- Model predictive control for energy optimization
- Pre-conditioning before charging/discharging
- Emergency cooling for thermal runaway prevention

Thermal models:
- Lumped capacitance (1D, 2D, 3D)
- Equivalent circuit thermal model
- CFD for detailed pack design
- Real-time simplified models for BMS

Performance targets:
- Temperature uniformity: ΔT < 5°C across pack
- Operating range: 20-35°C optimal
- Max cell temp: 60°C absolute limit
- Heating power: 2-5 kW, Cooling: 5-10 kW

skills.name: automotive-battery-lifecycle-battery-disassembly-automation
skills.title: Recycling
skills.description: Expert knowledge of robotic disassembly systems for battery packs including module separation, high-voltage safety, X-ray sorting, and barcode tracking.
skills.content:
## 适用场景
- Automated battery pack disassembly line design
- Robotic cell removal and module separation
- High-voltage safety interlocks and discharge systems
- X-ray and vision-based pack inspection
- Barcode tracking for traceability and chemistry sorting

## 相关标准
- ISO 12100 Machinery Safety
- ISO/TS 15066 Collaborative Robots
- IEC 61508 Functional Safety for automation
- ISO 17367 Battery Safety Handling
- ATEX Directive for explosion protection

## 约束
- CAPEX ($3-5M) requires high throughput (>25k packs/year) for ROI
- 50+ pack designs from OEMs require flexible tooling or multiple lines
- Adhesive-bonded packs difficult to automate (require thermal or ultrasonic cutting)
- X-ray inspection expensive ($500k+) but valuable for safety screening
- Vision algorithms require training data (1000+ images per pack variant)

## 推荐工具
- Industrial robots (articulated, gantry, or collaborative)
- Vision systems (2D, 3D, thermal cameras)
- Automatic tool changers and custom end-effectors
- Discharge equipment with load banks and monitoring
- Barcode/QR scanners for traceability
- PLC/SCADA for line control and data logging

## 方法
## Core Competencies
Expert in designing and implementing automated robotic systems for safe, efficient disassembly of automotive battery packs to recover modules, cells, and materials while maintaining worker safety and chemistry traceability.
### Disassembly Challenges
**Manual Disassembly Issues**: - Labor-intensive: 15-45 min per pack (cost $20-60) - Safety risks: High-voltage exposure (400-800V), thermal runaway potential - Inconsistent quality: Human error in module damage, incomplete discharge - Scalability limits: Trained technicians scarce, throughput <20 packs/day/worker - Ergonomics: Heavy packs (200-700 kg), repetitive strain injuries
**Automation Benefits**: - Throughput: 50-200 packs/day per line (3-10x improvement) - Safety: Isolates humans from high-voltage and fire hazards - Consistency: Repeatable disassembly sequences, minimal module damage - Data capture: Automated barcode scanning, weight measurement, voltage logging - Cost reduction: 40-60% lower cost per pack at scale
### Automated Disassembly Process Flow
**Stage 1: Pack Identification & Intake**
**Barcode/QR Code Scanning**: - Vision system reads pack identifier (VIN-based or OEM code) - Database lookup: Chemistry (NMC811, LFP, NCA), voltage, module count, disassembly procedure - Decision: Route to appropriate station (chemistry-specific tooling)
**Weight & Dimension Verification**: - Load cells verify pack mass (detect internal damage, electrolyte leakage) - Laser/vision system measures dimensions (detect swelling, deformation) - Acceptance criteria: ±5% of nominal weight/size
**X-ray Inspection** (optional, high-value packs): - Computed Tomography (CT) scan or 2D X-ray - Detect: Internal shorts, cell swelling, dendrite growth, missing components - Benefit: Avoid opening damaged packs (fire risk), prioritize for direct shredding
**Stage 2: High-Voltage Discharge & Safety Lockout**
**Voltage Measurement**: - Robotic arm connects to HV+ and HV- terminals via insulated probe - Measure pack voltage (should be <100V if pre-discharged, up to 400-800V if not) - Decision: If >100V, route to discharge station; if <50V, proceed to disassembly
**Active Discharge**: - Connect pack to resistive load bank (1-10 kW) - Discharge to 30-50% SOC (not 0% to avoid cell damage) - Time: 30 min to 4 hours depending on pack capacity (50-150 kWh) - Monitoring: Thermal camera detects cell hot spots (>40°C → abort)
**Safety Lockout**: - Remove service disconnect plug (robotic gripper with 1000V insulation) - Install shorting plug on HV terminals (prevent residual voltage) - Verify <50V with second independent measurement (redundant safety)
**Stage 3: Enclosure Removal (Pack Opening)**
**Bolt/Screw Removal**: - Robot arm with automatic tool changer (select screwdriver bit based on pack database) - Torque monitoring: Detect stripped threads, cross-threaded fasteners - Fastener sorting: Steel vs aluminum screws for recycling - Typical: 20-60 fasteners per pack (removal time: 3-8 min with multi-spindle tools)
**Adhesive/Sealant Cutting** (for glued enclosures): - Ultrasonic knife or hot wire cutter traces seam lines - Vision-guided path following (seam detection via machine learning) - Challenge: OEM-specific adhesives (polyurethane, epoxy, silicone) require different cutting strategies
**Lid Lift-off**: - Vacuum gripper or magnetic gripper lifts pack top cover (5-30 kg) - Place cover in parts bin (aluminum for recycling)
**Stage 4: BMS & Wiring Harness Removal**
**Connector Disconnection**: - Robot identifies connector types via vision (Molex, Amphenol, JST) - Custom end-effector with release mechanism (push-button, slide-lock, twist-lock) - Challenge: 50+ OEM-specific connector designs require modular grippers
**BMS PCB Extraction**: - Locate BMS board (typically bolted to pack lid or module top) - Unscrew mounting bolts (4-8 per BMS) - Lift BMS → route to electronics recycling (gold recovery from PCB)
**Cable Cutting**: - Automated wire cutters sever HV cables near bus bars - Copper cable → metal recovery stream - Benefit: Recover clean copper vs mixed in shredder
**Stage 5: Coolant Drainage** (liquid-cooled packs)
**Drain Port Access**: - Robot opens coolant drain valve or punctures coolant line - Pump drains coolant (ethylene glycol/water mix, 10-30 L per pack) - Coolant disposal: Recycle glycol or proper hazmat disposal
**Dry-out**: - Tilt pack to drain residual coolant (passive gravity drain for 5-10 min) - Compressed air purge of cooling channels (optional)
**Stage 6: Module Separation**
**Module Lifting**: - Robot gripper (vacuum cup arrays or mechanical clamps) lifts each module (10-40 kg) - Vision system locates module edges (handles dimensional variation between packs) - Lift sequence: Often back-to-front or top-to-bottom depending on pack design
**Bus Bar Disconnect**: - If modules series-connected via bus bars: robot cuts or unbolts bus bars - High-force cutting tool (hydraulic shear, 2-10 kN) for copper/aluminum bars - Safety: Verify 0V across bus bar before cutting (check for residual charge)
**Module Weight & Voltage Check**: - Each module placed on weighing station (QC check for internal damage) - Voltage measurement: Verify module is 20-50V (safe for handling) - Data logging: Module ID, weight, voltage → traceability database
**Chemistry Sorting**: - Based on pack ID or optional XRF analysis, route module to correct bin: - NMC811: Premium value, hydrometallurgy route - NMC622: Standard value, hydro or pyro - LFP: Low value, second-life or pyro - NCA: Tesla-specific, direct recycling pilot programs
**Stage 7: Cell Extraction** (optional, for second-life or direct recycling)
**Module Opening**: - Remove module plastic housing (snap fits or screws) - Expose cell pack (cylindrical 21700/4680 or pouch cells)
**Cell Removal**: - Cylindrical cells: Suction gripper with 18650/21700-sized cups - Pouch cells: Vacuum pad gripper (flexible to avoid puncture) - Welded tabs: Ultrasonic metal welder in reverse (melt and separate) or mechanical shear
**Cell Testing** (for second-life): - Automated cell tester measures: - Open-circuit voltage (OCV): Should be 3.0-4.2V for lithium-ion - Internal resistance (IR): <50 mΩ for good cell, >100 mΩ for degraded - Capacity test (optional, 1C discharge): Determines SOH - Sorting: Grade A (>80% SOH), Grade B (60-80%), Grade C (<60% → recycle)
### Robotic System Design
**Robot Selection**:
| Task | Robot Type | Payload | Reach | Speed | |------|-----------|---------|-------|-------| | Pack handling | Articulated 6-axis (KUKA, ABB, Fanuc) | 200-500 kg | 2.5-3.5 m | Slow (safety) | | Fastener removal | Collaborative robot (UR, Franka) | 5-15 kg | 1.3-1.8 m | Medium | | Module extraction | Gantry robot or Cartesian | 50-100 kg | 3-5 m XY, 1 m Z | Medium | | Cell handling | SCARA or delta robot | 1-5 kg | 0.8-1.5 m | Fast (precision) |
**End-Effectors (custom design critical)**: - Automatic tool changer: Quick swap between screwdriver, gripper, cutter, probe (30 sec changeover) - Screwdriver: Electric or pneumatic, torque monitoring (2-20 Nm range) - Gripper: Vacuum (for flat surfaces), magnetic (ferrous), mechanical (clamp) - Cutter: Hydraulic shear (bus bars), wire stripper (cables), ultrasonic knife (adhesive) - Probe: Insulated voltage measurement probe (1000V rated), temperature sensor
**Vision Systems**: - 2D cameras: Barcode reading, connector identification, module edge detection - 3D cameras (structured light, stereo): Bolt head location, deformation detection - Thermal cameras: Hot spot detection during discharge, cell temperature monitoring - X-ray: Internal damage assessment (optional for high-value packs)
**Safety Systems**: - Light curtains: Stop robot if human enters work envelope - Emergency stop buttons: Every 3 meters around line perimeter - Fume extraction: Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at pack opening (electrolyte vapor risk) - Fire suppression: CO2 or water mist system triggered by smoke/temperature sensors - Electrical isolation: Robot controllers on separate circuit from HV discharge equipment
### Traceability & Data Management
**Battery Passport Integration**: - Scan pack QR code → retrieve battery passport data (chemistry, manufacturing date, OEM, vehicle VIN) - Log disassembly data: Discharge voltage, module weights, visual damage observations - Update passport: "End-of-life → recycling, date: 2026-03-19, facility: XYZ"
**Chemistry Tracking**: - Critical for maximizing recycling value (NMC811 vs LFP routing) - Database stores: Pack ID → chemistry → module bin assignment - Enables: Homogenous feedstock to hydrometallurgy (avoids chemistry mixing)
**Module-to-Cell Lineage**: - Each module gets unique ID (laser-etched or RFID tag) - Cell testing results linked to module ID → informs second-life applications - Enables warranty tracking for second-life products
### Economics of Automated Disassembly
**CAPEX (for 50k pack/year line)**: - Robots & end-effectors: $1.5-2.5M (3-5 robots) - Vision systems: $200-500k - Discharge equipment: $300-600k - Conveyors & material handling: $400-700k - Safety systems & enclosures: $300-500k - Control system & software: $200-400k - Total CAPEX: $3-5M
**OPEX (per pack)**: - Labor: $5-10 (1 operator supervising 4-6 robots) - Energy: $2-4 (robot power, discharge energy recovery possible) - Maintenance: $3-5 (tool wear, robot servicing) - Total OPEX: $10-19 per pack
**Comparison to Manual**: - Manual: $30-60 per pack - Automated: $10-19 per pack - Savings: 50-70% at 50k+ pack/year scale
**Payback Period**: - At 50k packs/year: 3-4 years - At 100k packs/year: 2-3 years - Break-even: ~25k packs/year
### Case Studies
- **Duesenfeld (Germany)**: Fully automated line with LN2 cooling, 3k ton/year, 96% recovery rate - **OnTo Technology (USA)**: Collaborative robots (UR) for module extraction, BMW partnership - **Li-Cycle (Canada)**: Semi-automated discharge + manual disassembly, 25k ton/year - **Northvolt (Sweden)**: Gigafactory recycling plant, automated disassembly planned for 125k ton/year by 2030
## Approach
1. **Pack Portfolio Analysis**: Catalog OEM pack designs (fastener types, module layouts, chemistries) 2. **Disassembly Sequence Planning**: CAD simulation of robot paths, collision avoidance 3. **End-Effector Design**: Custom grippers for highest-volume pack types (Pareto 80/20 rule) 4. **Safety Risk Assessment**: HAZOP analysis of discharge, cutting, lifting operations 5. **Pilot Line Setup**: Build 1-station prototype, validate cycle time and safety 6. **Vision Algorithm Training**: Machine learning for connector/bolt detection (requires 1000+ images per variant) 7. **Scale-Up Design**: Multi-station line with buffer storage, throughput balancing 8. **Economic Modeling**: CAPEX, OPEX, throughput sensitivity analysis
## Deliverables
- Disassembly sequence flowchart for top 10 pack types - Robot selection justification (payload, reach, speed requirements) - End-effector CAD designs with force analysis - Safety system specification (light curtains, e-stops, fire suppression) - Vision system requirements (resolution, frame rate, lighting) - Traceability database schema (pack ID, module ID, test results) - Line layout (floor plan, robot work envelopes, material flow) - Economic model (CAPEX, OPEX per pack, payback period)
## Best Practices
- Design for flexibility: Use automatic tool changers to handle 80%+ of pack variants with same robot - Implement modular stations: Each station (discharge, opening, module extraction) can operate independently - Use collaborative robots where possible: Lower cost, easier programming, safer human interaction - Capture data at every step: Voltage, weight, temperature → predictive analytics for future packs - Design for graceful degradation: If one robot fails, line continues at reduced throughput - Perform weekly torque calibration: Ensures fastener removal without stripping threads - Train vision systems with synthetic data: CAD-based image generation for rare pack variants - Implement closed-loop force control: Prevents module damage during extraction (esp. pouch cells)
## Integration with Automotive Workflow
- Accept whole battery packs from OEM collection networks with barcode intact - Scan and update battery passport at intake and completion - Route modules to second-life assembly lines or recycling based on SOH results - Provide module-level traceability for closed-loop cathode supply chains - Report disassembly data (module count, chemistry distribution) to OEM for EPR compliance

skills.name: automotive-battery-lifecycle-battery-passport-implementation
skills.title: Regulatory
skills.description: Expert in implementing digital battery passports following GBA standard including data models, QR codes, blockchain traceability, and API integration with manufacturing systems.
skills.content:
## 适用场景
- Battery passport IT architecture design
- GBA data model implementation
- QR code generation and laser marking
- Blockchain/DLT for tamper-proof records
- MES/PLM integration for automated data capture

## 相关标准
- GBA (Global Battery Alliance) Battery Passport
- EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 Article 13
- ISO/IEC 15459 Unique Identifier Standards
- ISO/IEC 19762 AIDC Data Structures
- GDPR for data privacy

## 约束
- Data security vs transparency tradeoff (GDPR compliance)
- Blockchain gas costs for on-chain storage (prefer off-chain with hash)
- Supplier data quality varies (manual data entry errors)
- QR code durability over 15+ year battery life (corrosion, fading)
- API scalability for millions of batteries (load balancing required)

## 推荐工具
- Battery passport platform (Circulor, Minespider, SAP, custom)
- Blockchain (Hyperledger Fabric, Ethereum, or similar DLT)
- MES/PLM integration middleware
- Laser marking systems for QR codes
- Cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP)
- API gateway and authentication (OAuth 2.0, JWT)

## 方法
Expert in technical implementation of digital battery passports meeting EU Regulation requirements and GBA standard. Covers data architecture (70+ fields: manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, carbon footprint, recycled content, supply chain, performance, disassembly), unique identifier generation (ISO 15459 compliance), QR code standards (data matrix ECC200, laser etching on pack housing), backend systems (cloud database, API endpoints for authorized access), blockchain integration (Hyperledger, Ethereum for immutable provenance), MES/PLM integration (auto-capture manufacturing data: test results, traceability lots, assembly date), access control (GDPR-compliant multi-level: public chemistry/weight, OEM performance data, recycler disassembly info), lifecycle updates (SOH from vehicle telematics, service events, battery swap history), and end-of-life data (collection date, recycling facility, material recovery yields). Implementation phases: pilot (100 batteries, validate data flows), scale (1000s/month, load testing), full production (integrate into all manufacturing lines). Key technical decisions: centralized vs distributed storage, on-chain vs off-chain data (gas costs), API rate limiting, data retention policy (lifetime + 15 years post-recycling). Tools: SAP Product Compliance, Circulor Responsible Sourcing, Minespider blockchain platform, custom REST APIs, laser marking systems (fiber laser 20W), vision verification (OCR check QR readability post-marking). Cost: €10-30 per battery (IT amortization, laser marking, data entry/validation). Integration: Connects to vehicle CAN (SOH updates), recycler portals (EOL data input), regulatory reporting (annual compliance summaries). Best practices: Generate unique ID at cell level (propagate to module/pack), implement data validation hooks (prevent bad data entry), use industry PKI (trusted certificate authorities for API authentication), design for 20+ year data retention (archival strategy), test QR durability (salt spray, thermal cycling per ISO 11507).

- IEC 62133 Battery Safety Testing
- ISO 12100 Machinery Safety

## 约束
- Fire risk during shredding requires expensive safety systems
- Black mass price volatile (follows Co/Ni/Li commodity prices)
- Particle size control difficult (affects downstream leaching efficiency)
- Mixed chemistry feedstock reduces black mass grade and value
- Moisture control critical (hygroscopic, causes caking in storage)

## 推荐工具
- Hammer mill or shear shredder with ATEX certification
- ICP-OES or XRF for elemental analysis
- Laser diffraction particle size analyzer
- Moisture analyzer (loss on drying oven)
- Density separator or air classifier
- Off-gas treatment (thermal oxidizer or scrubber)

## 方法
## Core Competencies
Expert in mechanical processing of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries to produce black mass (fine powder containing cathode and anode active materials) for downstream pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical recycling.
### Black Mass Definition
